text.tspan: The exceptional performance of the 33‑metre twin conical chimneys at the National Palace of Sintra relies entirely on
the buoyancy‑driven physics of the stack effect (chimney effect). The chimneys create a high‑velocity air draft because
the column of air inside is significantly hotter and less dense than the cold outside air.
This density difference generates a natural pressure differential Delta P between the bottom and top of the chimney:
# El Sótano 333 m Stack
- Height: H = 333 m
- Base radius: r_1 approx 101.1 m, A_1 approx 3.21times10^4 m^2
- Top radius: r_2 approx 27.6 m, A_2 approx 2.39times10^3 m^2
- Draft pressure: Delta P approx 1916 Pa
- Velocity: v approx 79 m/s
- Volumetric flow: Q approx 2.53times10^6 m^3/s
- Mechanical power: P approx 9.5 GW
# Twin Half-Height Stacks
- Height each: 166.5 m
- Combined power: P approx 6.8 GW
# Power Equivalents
- ≈ 9–10 fossil fuel stations (1 GW each
- ≈ 9–10 nuclear units (1 GW each)
- ≈ 3,000–3,500 UK wind turbines (~3 MW each)
# Environmental Concept
To reach T_i approx 473–573 K with minimal combustion:
- Use data-centre and industrial waste heat (40–60°C)
- Lift temperature via heat pumps to ~100–120°C
- Top up to ~200°C using renewable electricity or solar-thermal
- Integrate geothermal and thermal storage
- Apply recursive heat exchangers and gas filtration
- Exploit terracotta thermal mass to stabilise stack behaviour
Delta P = rho_o g H left(1 - frac T_o T_iright)
- Delta P: draft pressure (Pa)
- rho_o approx 1.2 kg/m^3: ambient air density
- g = 9.81 m/s^2: gravity
- H = 33 m: chimney height
- T_o: outside temperature (K)
- T_i: inside flue temperature (K)
Because g and rho_o are constants, Delta P scales linearly with H. A 33 m stack has several times
the draft of a short roof flue.
The pressure differential is converted into velocity: v = sqrt{2 g H left(frac T_i - T_o{T_oright)
The conical geometry obeys the continuity equation: Q = A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2
- Q: volumetric flow rate (m^3/s)
- A_1, v_1: area and velocity at base
- A_2, v_2: area and velocity at top
Because A_2 ll A_1, the gas accelerates strongly toward the exit, creating a jet that resists downdrafts.
Terracotta brick provides high thermal mass, keeping T_i elevated and stabilising Delta P and v.
El Sótano de las Golondrinas is an open‑air pit cave in Aquismón, San Luis Potosí, Mexico.
Its mouth is an undercut ellipse (≈49×62 m, widening to a room ≈303×135 m.
The freefall drop is ≈333 m from the lowest side, making it the largest known cave shaft in the world.
Using area‑equivalent circular radii:
- Base: r_1 approx 101.1 m, A_1 = pi r_1^2 approx 3.21times10^4 m^2
- Top: r_2 approx 27.6 m, A_2 = pi r_2^2 approx 2.39times10^3 m^2
Estimated void volume: V approx 4.8times10^6 m^3
With H = 333 m, T_o = 293 K, T_i = 573 K, rho_o = 1.2 kg/m^3:
Delta P approx 1916 Pa,quad v approx 79 m/s,quad Q approx 2.53times10^6 m^3/s
Mechanical power: P approx frac{1{2rho_o Q v^2 approx 9.5 GW
Twin half‑height stacks (166.5 m each) give ≈3.4 GW per tower, ≈6.8 GW combined.
Analogies for Q approx 2.53times10^6 m^3/s:
- Small tornado core
- Filling a football stadium every second
- Half the Thames flow (in air)
- 1000 cooling towers
- Two Shard skyscrapers per second
Structurally, a conceptual terracotta shell might be:
- Single 333 m stack: 8–10 m thick at base, tapering to 2–3 m at top
- Twin 166.5 m stacks: 5–7 m at base, ~2 m at top
Environmentally, to reach T_i approx 473 K at the base with minimal combustion:
- Use waste heat (data centres, industry) at 40–60°C
- Lift temperature via heat pumps to ~100–120°C
- Top up to ~200°C with renewable electricity or solar‑thermal
- Employ geothermal and thermal storage
- Use recursive heat exchangers and gas filtration (NOₓ, SOₓ, particulates)
- Exploit terracotta thermal mass to stabilise temperature
Data‑centre waste heat can’t alone reach 200°C, but it significantly reduces additional energy needed
and integrates into a low‑carbon thermal ecosystem.
